My family has worked this land for three generations. I am 63 now, my knees hurt in the cold, and I cannot afford to gamble. I know what this land gives back.

**Wheat first.** It is always wheat. Every family in our village grows winter wheat — you sow it in October, and by June you have something to sell and something to eat. I use the county seed station's improved variety, the same Jimai kind I've been using for years. My neighbor switched to some new variety last year and got a poorer stand in the cold snap. I will not do that. I put down base fertilizer before plowing — diammonium phosphate and urea mixed together — then top-dress urea at jointing stage. I irrigate four times: once at sowing to get germination, once before winter, once at jointing, once at heading. That is what my father did and what the yields tell me is right. I spray herbicide in winter when the weeds are small, then treat for aphids and rust in spring. Maybe three spray rounds total.

**Then maize on the same land after wheat harvest.** No gap — I seed directly into the stubble to save time and cost. I buy hybrid seed from the market, Xianyu or Zhengdan type, because everybody knows hybrid corn outyields traditional. Summer rains help a lot, so I only irrigate once at silking if July is dry. Maize gets less fertilizer than wheat from me — it rains more in summer, leaching is a problem, and I have seen my neighbors burn their stands by overdoing it.

I have about 10 mu total. I plant all of it in this rotation — wheat in winter, maize in summer. I cannot afford to leave land idle.
